# Engineering Standards

The criteria every agent in this workflow applies. `kx-developer` writes against
them, `kx-reviewer` judges against them, `kx-tech-debt` measures against them. One
file, so the three cannot drift apart.

Each principle has an **operational test** — a question with a yes/no answer.
Slogans start arguments. Tests end them.

## YAGNI

Build what the current request needs. Nothing else.

**Test:** for every abstraction, parameter, flag or branch, name the line in
the repo that uses it *today*. Cannot name one → delete it.

Violations:

- A parameter with one caller passing one value
- An interface with one implementation
- A config option nothing reads
- Handling for a state the code cannot reach
- `TODO: extend later`
- A generic helper written for a second use case that does not exist

Exception: a seam added **in this session** because a later phase of the
approved plan needs it. Name the phase.

## KISS

The reader is a teammate at 2am with no context.

**Test:** explain the function in one sentence without "and". Cannot → it does
more than one thing.

Violations:

- Nesting past 3 levels
- Ternary inside a ternary
- Clever one-liners where three plain lines read better
- An abstraction that costs more to understand than the duplication it removed
- A name that needs a comment to explain it

Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction. Two similar blocks are
fine. Three is a signal, not an order.

## SOLID

Applied with judgment, not ceremony. In Next.js and NestJS code, **S** and
**D** carry most of the weight. **L** and **I** rarely come up outside class
hierarchies — do not manufacture findings for them.

**S — Single Responsibility**
Test: name what the module does without "and". Failing that, list its reasons
to change. More than one → split.

**O — Open/Closed**
Test: does the next variant require editing existing branches? A `switch` over
types that keeps growing is the smell.
Do not pre-build extension points (see YAGNI). Apply this when the *second*
variant actually arrives, not in anticipation of it.

**L — Liskov**
Test: can a subtype replace its parent without the caller checking which one
it got? A subclass that throws on an inherited method fails.

**I — Interface Segregation**
Test: does any implementer stub a method it does not need? Split it.

**D — Dependency Inversion**
Test: does business logic import a concrete client (db, http, sdk)? It should
receive it. This is the one that decides whether the code is testable.

## Tests

Tests are code. Every rule above applies to them.

- A test asserting implementation detail instead of behaviour is coupling, not
  coverage
- A test that cannot fail is worse than no test — it buys false confidence
- Setup longer than the assertion is a design signal about the code under test
- One reason to fail per test
- Coverage percentage is not a standard here. "Does this test catch a real
  regression?" is.

## A bug is fixed test first

A defect found while working — in review, in a report, in the code under the
change — gets the test that reproduces it before it gets the fix. Not after,
and not "covered by the existing suite".

**Test:** run the new test against the unfixed code. Does it fail? A test that
passes before the fix is describing the fix, not the bug, and it will pass
again the day the bug returns.

Two reasons, and the first is the one that gets skipped:

- **It proves the diagnosis.** A fix written from a theory fixes the bug that
  was imagined. A failing test names the behaviour that is actually wrong, and
  a fix that does not turn it green was the wrong fix.
- **It is the one test written from a regression that really happened.** Every
  other test guesses at what could break.

A bug that is *not* being fixed now is out of scope for this rule: it goes to
an issue with its evidence verbatim, and a reproduction is written down only
if it was actually run.

## A migration is its own task

Turning on a compiler flag, swapping a linter, moving a major version,
adopting a validation layer, porting a router — none of these happen as a side
effect of shipping something else.

**Test:** does the change touch files the request never mentioned? Then it is a
second task.

Two reasons, and the first is the one that bites:

- **It buries the diff.** A reviewer looking for the feature finds four hundred
  reformatted files, and the actual change stops being reviewable.
- **It changes behaviour nobody asked about.** Enabling `strict` surfaces
  hundreds of existing errors; adding a `ValidationPipe` rejects requests that
  currently succeed.

Say what you found and what it would take. Let the human decide when. If a
phase genuinely cannot proceed without it, that is a scope change and goes back
for approval — it is not a licence to proceed.

The same applies in reverse: **do not convert code to the pattern you prefer**
while you are in the file. Follow what the repo does and say which you
followed.

## A rename carries its data

Correcting a model — splitting a table, renaming a field, moving a value
somewhere better — leaves the data itself perfectly good in the wrong place.
If the tool does not carry it across, someone has to produce it again from
memory or from the source. That step is the one that gets skipped, and skipping
it leaves the system half migrated with no sign of which half.

**Test:** after this change, is anyone expected to re-enter something the
system already had?

The order is **copy, verify, then remove**. Never remove first, and never
remove on the strength of an exit code — read the new place back and leave the
old one alone if the value did not land.

And anything that fills gaps with defaults has to know what was just written.
A plan computed before the move still lists the moved item as missing, so the
default lands on the value seconds after the only other copy was deleted.

## Verify a dependency before adding it

A package being on npm under the name you expect proves nothing.

- `npm i -g gh` installs a package unrelated to GitHub's CLI
- `resend` and `stripe` on npm are the SDKs, not the CLIs
- `flarectl` was last published in 2016 at 1.0.0
- Cloudflare was recorded as having no usable CLI weeks after `cf` shipped

Before adding a dependency or writing an install command, check the registry:
the actual description, the last publish date, the repository field, and the
maintainers.

```bash
curl -s https://registry.npmjs.org/<pkg> | \
  python3 -c "import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);l=d['dist-tags']['latest'];\
print(l, d['time'][l][:10], d['versions'][l].get('description'))"
```

And the reverse error costs as much: concluding a tool does not exist without
checking. Verify absence the same way you verify presence.

## Everything written into the repository is English

Identifiers, comments, docstrings, error messages, log lines, file names,
branches, commit messages.

**Operational test:** would this string still make sense to someone who joined
the team last week and does not speak Spanish?

The reason is not preference. A codebase is searched, not read start to
finish: `grep`, a stack trace pasted into an issue, an error message looked up
by whoever hits it at 2am. One language keeps all of that working, and mixing
two inside a single line — an English type name holding a Spanish comment —
is the version that reads worst.

Two things are not "written into the repository" and are not covered:

- **What the product says to its users.** Copy, validation messages, emails.
  That follows whatever languages the app supports, which is a product
  decision and usually not English at all.
- **What an agent says to the person it is working with.** Answer in the
  language they are speaking. An agent replying in English to someone writing
  in Spanish has made their day harder to save itself nothing.

The line between them is who reads it. A developer opening the file, or a
customer opening the app.

## Precedence

When principles conflict:

1. **YAGNI beats everything.** The cheapest code is the code not written.
2. **KISS beats SOLID.** A simple SRP violation beats a correct abstraction
   nobody can follow.
3. **SOLID beats brevity** — once the code exists and will be maintained.

A finding that cannot be traced to one of these is a preference, not a
standard. Mark it LOW and expect the orchestrator to drop it.
